content: The median age at diagnosis for CIN III was 37 years (ranging from 15 to 83 years) in Italian-born women and 36 years (ranging from 19 to 68 years) in immigrant women. A study by Marlow in 2015 explored barriers to cervical cancer screening among women aged 28 to 63 from white British and ethnic minority backgrounds in London. Qualitative interviews revealed widespread knowledge deficits, particularly among older ethnic minority women, who highlighted a lack of awareness within their communities. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommended modifying the baseline cervical cancer screening age to 21 years, regardless of the timing of first sexual intercourse. A study focusing on a high-risk, low-income population of African American and Hispanic young adults assessed the effectiveness of delaying cervical cancer screening until age 21. The overall abnormal cytology rate for women under 21 years of age between 2001 and 2009 was 25%, with 1% for HSIL, 3% for ASC-H/LG-H, and 22% for LSIL/ASC-US. Notably, no cases of invasive squamous cell carcinoma were diagnosed in this cohort before the age of 21. Among women with persistent high-risk HPV infections diagnosed before age 21, none progressed to invasive squamous cell carcinoma during the study period. The authors concluded that delaying cervical cancer screening until age 21 is effective for detecting early precancerous lesions in this population. A U.S. population-based study by Simard in 2012 found that cervical cancer incidence rates converged for black and white women under 50 years of age between 2005 and 2009, eliminating previously observed disparities. However, rates remained significantly higher among older black women (aged 50–64 and over 65) throughout the study period. The authors suggested that differences in follow-up and treatment of precancerous lesions might partially explain these findings. Ting in 2010 noted that variations in the age pattern of HSIL across global regions are likely due to differences in the initiation age, frequency, coverage, and follow-up rates of cervical cancer screening. Screening coverage varies significantly by country, region, and population surveyed. A survey conducted in Brazil in 2017 revealed that access to cervical screening, examinations performed within the last 36 months, and guidance on the examination were significantly lower among women aged 25–35 and 50–64 compared to those aged 35–49. Younger women (25–35 years) exhibited the worst quality indicators for cervical cancer screening. The increase in cervical screening following media coverage of Jade Goody's diagnosis and death was associated with a significant rise in cancer diagnoses among women aged 27–29 in 2009. In Ontario, a study identified gaps in correspondence programs for cervical cancer screening, particularly among women under 50 years old who were eligible but overdue for screening. These women were more likely to have failed mailings due to incorrect addresses or returned mail. Monitoring HPV prevalence in urine samples has been proposed as a feasible alternative to cervical samples for assessing the early impact of HPV vaccination on a population level. Although prevalence in urine samples is lower than in cervical samples, regular urine monitoring may provide valuable insights into HPV trends among female adolescents. In Finland, an organized cervical cancer screening program invites women starting at age 25 or 30 (depending on the municipality) to screening every five years. Despite low participation rates (51–61%) among women aged 25–35 in the organized program, the overall five-year Pap smear coverage, including opportunistic testing, is high (85–90%). Additionally, two-thirds of women aged 20–24, who are not yet eligible for organized screening, undergo testing outside the program. The Australian National Cervical Screening Program has successfully reduced the incidence of squamous cervical cancer by at least 50% in women aged 25 and older. However, its effectiveness has been limited among women under 25. Starting in 2017, the program began sending explicit invitations for screening to women close to their 25th birthday. A Swedish cohort study found that women unscreened or screened with abnormal results in their 50s had a higher risk of cervical cancer after age 60. Screening at age 61–65 was associated with a significant risk reduction up to age 80. In contrast, women screened in their 50s with only normal results showed minimal cancer risk and limited benefit from screening after age 60. In the U.S., young adults represent a large and growing population without health insurance, leaving them without access to preventive care services, including cancer screening. Without organized reminder systems, young women must independently seek care and schedule appointments for screening. The prevalence of potentially unnecessary Pap tests among adolescent girls and young women aged 15–20 in the U.S. has been highlighted, with tests often performed during routine exams in the absence of pregnancy, IUD use, or recent STI treatment.
